title: Video-call therapy and anxiety
claim: therapy delivered by video call is as effective as face-to-face therapy for treating anxiety

sources.title: Clinic records: final anxiety scores by mode of therapy
text: A mental health clinic in Abu Dhabi reviewed the records of 212 adults who completed a 10-session course of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for anxiety between 2023 and 2025. Patients chose whether to attend sessions in person (131 patients) or by video call (81 patients). Anxiety was measured at the end of treatment with the GAD-7, a questionnaire scored from 0 to 21, where higher scores indicate more severe anxiety. Figure 1 shows the mean final score for each group.

figure.title: Figure 1: Mean anxiety score at the end of CBT, by mode of therapy
figure.yLabel: Mean GAD-7 score at end of treatment

sources.title: Randomised trial of video-call and face-to-face CBT
text: Researchers in Dubai recruited 96 adults aged 19 to 54 who had been diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder at two outpatient clinics. Participants were randomly allocated to 12 weekly sessions of CBT, delivered either face-to-face at the clinic or by secure video call from home. The same six therapists delivered both conditions and followed the same treatment manual.

Anxiety was measured with the GAD-7 (0 to 21, higher scores indicate more severe anxiety) before treatment and after the final session. A score below 8 was counted as recovery. Participants who attended fewer than 8 sessions were counted as having dropped out, and only those who completed treatment were included in the comparison of scores.

Both groups' scores fell significantly from before to after treatment (p < 0.001). An independent-samples t-test comparing the two groups' scores after treatment found t(81) = 0.80, p = 0.43. The critical value of t at p < 0.05 is 1.99.

table.caption: Table 1: Drop-out and GAD-7 scores by condition (SD in brackets)

sources.title: Clients' experiences of video-call therapy
text: A clinical psychologist working at a tele-therapy service in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, interviewed 12 clients (7 women and 5 men, aged 18 to 30, all Saudi nationals) who had completed at least 10 video-call CBT sessions for anxiety. Clients were invited to take part by their own therapists. The psychologist had been the therapist for 4 of the 12 clients. Clients who had stopped therapy early were not contacted.

The semi-structured interviews lasted about 30 minutes, were carried out by video call in Arabic and were audio-recorded. The psychologist translated the transcripts into English and carried out a thematic analysis on her own. Interviewing stopped after the twelfth interview because no new ideas were appearing.
themes: Theme 1: Convenience and access. Clients valued not having to travel and being able to fit sessions around university or work.
Theme 2: Home as a safe but crowded space. Being at home felt comfortable, but finding privacy from family members was sometimes difficult.
Theme 3: Connection through the screen. Most clients felt understood by their therapist, although some said trust took longer to build and technical problems interrupted difficult moments.

quotes.text: I could have my session in my car outside the university and still be on time for my lecture.
At home my younger brothers would knock on the door, so I sometimes kept my answers short.
When the screen froze in the middle of something difficult, I lost what I was trying to say.
After the third session it felt the same as sitting in a room with her.

sources.title: Conditions of online therapy and improvement in adolescents
text: Researchers surveyed 386 adolescents aged 14 to 18 in Saudi Arabia and Oman who had received at least six sessions of online video-call therapy for anxiety through school counselling services or private clinics.

Participants completed questionnaires measuring therapeutic alliance (how strongly they felt they and their therapist were working together, scored 0 to 60), how often their sessions were disrupted by connection problems, and whether they had a private room for sessions. Improvement was calculated as the fall in their GAD-7 anxiety score (0 to 21) from the start of therapy to the time of the survey, so a higher number means more improvement.

table.caption: Table 2: Factors related to improvement in anxiety during online therapy

sources.title: Exposure-based therapy for social anxiety in person and by video
text: Researchers in the United Kingdom randomly allocated 120 adults with social anxiety disorder to 14 sessions of CBT that included exposure exercises, either in person or by video call. In the in-person condition, therapists sometimes accompanied clients on exposure tasks in public places such as shops and cafés. In the video-call condition, clients carried out the same exposure tasks alone and discussed them with the therapist in the next session.

Symptoms were measured with a social anxiety rating scale (0 to 144, higher scores indicate more severe symptoms) before treatment, at the end of treatment and six months later. Of the 120 participants, 106 completed all three measurements (54 in person, 52 by video call). The critical value of t at p < 0.05 is 1.98.

table.caption: Table 3: Mean social anxiety scores (SD in brackets)

questions.text: Explain one issue that limits the interpretation of the data in source 1.
Analyse the findings from source 2 and state a conclusion linked to the claim that therapy delivered by video call is as effective as face-to-face therapy for treating anxiety.
Discuss how the researcher could improve the credibility of the findings in source 3.

To what extent can we conclude that therapy delivered by video call is as effective as face-to-face therapy for treating anxiety? In your answer, use your own knowledge and at least three of sources 2 to 5.

issues: The y-axis starts at 7 rather than 0, so a difference of 0.8 points on a 0 to 21 scale is drawn so that the video-call bar looks more than twice as tall as the face-to-face bar, exaggerating how much worse video-call patients appear to be.
Because the axis only covers 7 to 9, the reader cannot see where these scores sit on the full GAD-7 range, so it is hard to judge that both groups ended treatment with similar, fairly mild scores.

No error bars or standard deviations are shown, so it is impossible to tell how much individual scores varied or whether the two distributions overlap heavily, which they are likely to do with a difference of under one point.
Only end-of-treatment scores are shown, with no starting scores, so the figure cannot show how much each group improved; a group that started more anxious could end higher while improving more.
The groups are unequal in size (131 and 81) and this is not shown on the figure, so the mean for the smaller video-call group is less stable and could be pulled up by a few high scores.
Means alone may hide skewed distributions, so the figure does not show whether a typical patient in each group scored similarly.

analysis: Before treatment the groups were very similar (14.2 and 14.5, SDs about 3), suggesting random allocation produced comparable groups.
Both groups improved by a similar amount: face-to-face scores fell by 6.6 points and video-call scores by 6.2 points, and both falls were significant (p < 0.001).
After treatment the difference between groups was only 0.7 points, small relative to the SDs (3.8 and 4.2) and the overlapping ranges (1 to 17 and 0 to 19).
The between-group test was not significant: t(81) = 0.80 is well below the critical value of 1.99 (p = 0.43), so the small difference could easily be due to chance.
Recovery rates were similar: 56% (22 of 39) face-to-face and 52% (23 of 44) by video call.

Drop-out was lower for video call (4 of 48, about 8%) than face-to-face (9 of 48, about 19%); because only completers were compared, the score comparison does not include the people who left treatment.
conclusion: The findings provide support for the claim: adults with generalised anxiety improved by a similar amount with video-call CBT as with face-to-face CBT, and the difference after treatment was small and not significant.
A cautious conclusion is that, in this sample, there is no evidence that video-call CBT was less effective, although a non-significant difference does not prove the two are equally effective.
The lower drop-out in the video-call group suggests it may be at least as acceptable to patients, which partly supports the claim about overall effectiveness.

points: Researcher triangulation: a second researcher, not employed by the service, could code the transcripts independently and the two could compare and agree themes, reducing the influence of one person's interpretation.

The psychologist had been the therapist for 4 of the 12 clients; an independent interviewer with no link to the service would make it easier for clients to describe negative experiences, increasing the credibility of the positive themes.

Reflexivity: as an employee of a tele-therapy service, the psychologist has an interest in it working, so she could keep a reflexive journal and report how her role may have shaped the questions and the coding.
Member checking: summaries of each interview, or the draft themes, could be returned to clients to confirm they reflect what they meant.

Translation: transcripts were translated from Arabic by the same psychologist; a bilingual second researcher could check the translations, or the analysis could be done in Arabic, so that meaning is not lost or altered.

Data triangulation: clients who stopped therapy early were not contacted and clients were invited by their own therapists, so including drop-outs, therapists' views or GAD-7 scores would test whether the themes hold across different sources.

The claim of saturation after 12 interviews could be supported more convincingly by interviewing clients with different experiences, for example those who had frequent technical problems or lived in crowded homes.

sources: Source 2 supports the claim: in a randomised trial, video-call and face-to-face CBT produced similar improvements and recovery rates for generalised anxiety, with lower drop-out for video call. Limitation: a non-significant result does not prove equivalence, and only completers were analysed.

Source 3 partly supports the claim: clients valued convenience and most felt connected, but privacy at home and technical problems could limit what they disclosed. Limitation: 12 clients who completed therapy, recruited by their own therapists and interviewed by a psychologist linked to the service.

Source 4 complicates the claim: online therapy worked better for adolescents with a strong therapeutic alliance, few connection problems and a private room, suggesting effectiveness depends on conditions at home. Limitation: correlational, self-report and no face-to-face comparison group.

Source 5 challenges the claim: for social anxiety with exposure tasks, video call was similar at the end of treatment but significantly less effective six months later. Limitation: one disorder and one treatment type in the UK; the conditions also differed in whether the therapist accompanied exposure.
discussion: Whether the claim holds may depend on the type of anxiety and treatment: CBT for generalised anxiety seems to transfer well to video call (Sources 2 and 3), but exposure-based treatment for social anxiety may not (Source 5).

Short-term versus long-term effectiveness: Source 5 shows no significant difference at the end of treatment but a difference after six months, so studies that measure only at the end of treatment may overstate equivalence.
Effectiveness depends on practical conditions such as privacy, internet quality and the therapeutic alliance (Sources 3 and 4), which are unequally distributed between families and countries.

Lower drop-out with video call (Source 2) and convenience (Source 3) suggest tele-therapy may reach people who would otherwise not complete treatment, which matters for effectiveness at a population level.

Methodological points: randomised designs (Sources 2 and 5) allow stronger conclusions than self-selected or correlational data (Sources 1 and 4); 'no significant difference' is not the same as 'as effective'.
Generalisability across age and culture: the sources include Gulf adults, Saudi young adults, adolescents in Saudi Arabia and Oman and UK adults, so the claim may need to be qualified by population.
ownKnowledge: Cognitive behavioural therapy (Beck) and the role of homework and exposure in treating anxiety, which may be harder to support remotely.
Meta-analyses of guided internet-delivered CBT (for example Andersson and colleagues, 2014) reporting broadly similar outcomes to face-to-face CBT for several disorders.
The therapeutic alliance (Bordin's working alliance) and common factors explanations of why different forms of therapy often produce similar outcomes.
Barriers to help-seeking such as stigma, cost and travel, which tele-therapy may reduce, and the digital divide, which may limit access for some groups.
The difference between efficacy in controlled trials and effectiveness in everyday clinical settings.

q1: I identified one specific issue with how Figure 1 presents the data, not a problem with how the study was designed.
I pointed out that the y-axis starts at 7, not 0, and explained how this makes the 0.8-point difference look much larger.
I used the actual numbers (7.6 and 8.4 on a 0 to 21 scale) to show how small the real difference is.
I explained what a reader might wrongly conclude because of this issue.
I did not write a list of several issues; I developed one issue fully.
q2: I compared the before and after means for both groups and calculated how much each group improved.
I used the SDs and the ranges to comment on the overlap between the two groups after treatment.
I compared t = 0.80 with the critical value of 1.99 and explained what a non-significant result means.
I used the drop-out and recovery figures, not just the means.
I stated a conclusion that refers to the claim and to these specific findings.
I did not say the study proves the two therapies are equally effective.
q3: I explained how at least two specific changes would improve credibility, for example an independent interviewer or a second coder.
I referred to specific details in Source 3, such as the psychologist being the therapist for 4 clients or translating the transcripts herself.
I explained why each change would make the findings more believable, not just named the technique.
I discussed who was left out (clients who stopped therapy early) and how including them would test the themes.
I wrote in developed paragraphs, not a numbered list.
q4: I used at least three of Sources 2 to 5 and said what each suggests about the claim.
I evaluated each source I used, for example its design, sample or how long after treatment it measured outcomes.
I discussed the point of view that video call is as effective (Sources 2 and 3) and the point of view that it depends or is less effective (Sources 4 and 5).
I noticed that Source 5 shows a difference at six months but not at the end of treatment.
I brought in my own knowledge, for example CBT, exposure therapy, the therapeutic alliance or the digital divide.
I ended with a reasoned conclusion that qualifies the claim (for which disorders, people and conditions).

areaOfInquiry: The effect of technology on attachment
title: Parents' phones and attachment
claim: parents' smartphone use during time with their children weakens attachment between parents and young children

sources.title: Parents' phone use and children's attachment classification
text: Researchers in Dubai and Sharjah asked parents of children aged 2 to 4 how often they used their smartphone while looking after their child. Trained observers then watched each child during a short separation from and reunion with the parent in a playroom, and classified the child as securely or insecurely attached. Figure 1 shows the percentage of children classified as securely attached in each phone-use category.

figure.title: Figure 1: Children classified as securely attached, by parent's reported phone use while caring for the child
figure.xLabel: Parent's reported phone use while caring for the child

sources.title: Toddlers' behaviour when a parent uses a phone
text: Researchers in Abu Dhabi observed 40 parent and child pairs (28 mothers and 12 fathers; children aged 12 to 24 months, mean 17.5 months) in a university playroom. Each pair took part in three phases of 3 minutes (180 seconds) in a fixed order. In the free play phase, the parent played with the child as normal. In the phone phase, the parent read and replied to messages on their phone and responded to the child only if necessary. In the reunion phase, the parent put the phone away and played with the child again.

Two observers who did not know the aims of the study coded video recordings for: seconds of negative emotion (fussing or crying), the number of bids for attention (calling, touching or showing toys to the parent) and seconds spent exploring toys. Agreement between the observers was 0.89. Paired t-tests compared each phase with free play (critical value of t(39) at p < 0.05 = 2.02).

table.caption: Table 1: Mean child behaviour in each phase (SD in brackets), with paired t-tests against free play

sources.title: Parents talk about phones and family time
text: A researcher in Muscat, Oman, who runs a parenting workshop programme promoting screen-free family time, interviewed 16 parents (11 mothers and 5 fathers) of children aged 1 to 5. Participants were recruited from parents who had signed up for one of her workshops. Interviews took place in participants' homes, sometimes with the other parent present, and were carried out in Arabic or English depending on the parent's preference.

The interview schedule opened with the question: "How do you think your phone use affects your child?" Interviews lasted 40 to 60 minutes and were audio-recorded and transcribed. The researcher coded all the transcripts herself, searching for examples of how phone use affected the relationship between parent and child, and grouped these into themes.
themes: Theme 1: Guilt about divided attention. Most parents felt guilty when they used their phone while with their child.
Theme 2: Competing with the phone. Parents described children pushing phones away, asking to be picked up or giving up trying to talk to them.
Theme 3: The phone as a shared family activity. A smaller number of parents described using the phone with their child, for example video calls with grandparents or looking at family photos.

quotes.text: When I am on my phone, my daughter climbs onto my lap and pushes it away. She knows it takes me from her.
I answer work messages at dinner. My son has stopped telling me about his day because he thinks I am not listening.
I feel like a bad mother when I check my phone at the park.
Every evening we video call my mother in Salalah, and my son sits with me and talks to her. For us the phone brings the family together.

sources.title: Phone use, sensitivity and later attachment
text: A longitudinal study in Canada recruited 600 families with 9-month-old infants; 512 families completed both stages. When infants were 9 months old, parents reported how many minutes per day they used their smartphone while caring for their infant, and trained raters scored parental sensitivity (how quickly and appropriately the parent responded to the infant's signals) from video recordings of a feeding and play session.

When children were 24 months old, observers assessed attachment security at home using an attachment Q-sort, which gives a score from -1.0 to +1.0 (higher scores indicate more secure attachment). When parental sensitivity was statistically controlled, the correlation between phone use at 9 months and attachment security at 24 months fell to r = -0.03 (p = 0.50).

table.caption: Table 2: Correlations between the main measures (n = 512)
rows: Phone use at 9 months and attachment security at 24 months
Parental sensitivity at 9 months and attachment security at 24 months
Phone use at 9 months and parental sensitivity at 9 months

sources.title: Kinds of phone use and closeness to children
text: Researchers surveyed 350 parents of children aged 2 to 6 in Doha, Qatar; 217 of the parents (62%) were expatriates. For one week, parents kept a daily diary of their phone use while they were with their child. Researchers coded each entry as absorbed use (the parent using the phone alone, such as reading messages or scrolling) or shared use (using the phone together with the child, such as video calls with relatives, looking at family photos or singing along to songs).

Parents also completed a closeness questionnaire about their relationship with their child (scored 8 to 40, higher scores indicate a closer, warmer relationship). Correlations with an absolute value above 0.105 are significant at p < 0.05 for this sample.

table.caption: Table 3: Weekly phone use with the child and parent-rated closeness

questions.text: Explain one issue that limits the interpretation of the data in source 1.
Analyse the findings from source 2 and state a conclusion linked to the claim that parents' smartphone use during time with their children weakens attachment between parents and young children.
Discuss how the researcher could avoid bias in source 3.

To what extent can we conclude that parents' smartphone use during time with their children weakens attachment between parents and young children? In your answer, use your own knowledge and at least three of sources 2 to 5.

issues: The figure gives percentages but no number of children in each category, so the reader cannot tell whether 33% in the 'Almost always' group is based on a handful of children or many; with a very small group, one or two children changing classification would change the percentage greatly.

Groups based on how often parents use their phone are likely to be very unequal in size (few parents would report 'Almost always'), so the dramatic drop for the last bar may be the least reliable figure on the graph.
Without the counts, the reader cannot check the percentages or work out how many children in total were insecurely attached in each category.
No total sample size is given anywhere, so the reader cannot judge how much confidence to place in any of the differences between bars.
The categories ('Rarely' to 'Almost always') are not defined, so the reader cannot tell how much phone use each bar represents or whether parents interpreted them in the same way.
Each bar shows a percentage within its own category, so the bars do not add to 100%; a reader could misread them as the share of the whole sample.

analysis: During the phone phase, negative emotion rose from a mean of 8.2 to 31.5 seconds (almost four times as much), and t = 6.12 is far above the critical value of 2.02.
Bids for attention almost doubled (6.4 to 11.8) and toy exploration fell by about 37 seconds (121.3 to 84.6), both significant (t = 6.85 and 5.40).
The large SD for negative emotion in the phone phase (22.4, about 70% of the mean) suggests some children became very distressed while others reacted little.

In the reunion phase most behaviour returned close to free play levels: negative emotion (12.7) and exploration (112.0) were not significantly different from free play (t = 1.96 and 1.71, below 2.02).
Bids for attention stayed slightly but significantly higher in the reunion (7.9 vs 6.4, t = 2.31, p = 0.03), suggesting a small lasting effect within the session.
The source measures immediate behaviour over three minutes, not attachment classification, so conclusions about attachment go beyond the data.
conclusion: The findings partly support the claim: parents' phone use caused an immediate rise in toddlers' distress and attention seeking and less exploration, behaviours linked to the attachment system.
However, most behaviour recovered once the parent put the phone away, so the findings show a short-term disruption to interaction rather than a weakening of attachment itself.
A cautious conclusion is that brief phone use disrupts the secure-base behaviour of toddlers in the moment, but this source cannot show long-term effects on attachment.

points: Researcher bias: the researcher runs a programme promoting screen-free family time, so she may interpret answers to fit her view; an independent researcher with no stake in the programme could carry out the interviews and analysis, and she could practise reflexivity by recording her assumptions.

Confirmation bias in analysis: she coded the transcripts alone and searched specifically for effects of phone use on the relationship; a second, independent coder using an open, inductive approach, and comparing codes, would reduce this.

Leading question: the opening question assumes that phone use affects the child; neutral, open questions (for example asking parents to describe a typical evening) would reduce demand characteristics.

Sampling bias: participants had signed up for a screen-free workshop and may already be worried about phones; recruiting parents through other routes, such as nurseries or clinics, would give a wider range of views.

Social desirability: interviews at home with the other parent sometimes present may lead parents to give answers that make them look like good parents; interviewing parents individually and stressing confidentiality would reduce this.
The minority theme of shared phone use suggests views that did not fit the researcher's focus; actively seeking negative or contradictory cases would help avoid bias in which themes are reported.
Interviews in two languages coded by one person may introduce bias in interpretation; having bilingual researchers check translations and codes would help.

sources: Source 2 partly supports the claim: when parents used their phones, toddlers showed more distress and attention seeking and explored less. Limitation: a short laboratory task measuring immediate behaviour, not attachment, with a fixed order of phases.

Source 3 supports the claim from parents' perspectives (guilt, children competing with the phone) but also includes shared use that brings families together. Limitation: likely researcher and sampling bias, as the interviewer runs a screen-free programme and recruited from her workshops.

Source 4 complicates the claim: phone use predicted slightly less secure attachment (r = -0.14), but this disappeared once parental sensitivity was controlled, suggesting phone use matters mainly when it reduces sensitive responding. Limitation: correlational and self-reported phone use; Canadian sample.

Source 5 challenges a simple version of the claim: absorbed use was linked to less closeness, but shared use was linked to more, and total phone time was unrelated. Limitation: parent-rated closeness rather than an observed attachment measure, and correlational.
discussion: The type of phone use matters: absorbed use is linked to poorer outcomes (Sources 2 and 5) while shared use may strengthen family bonds (Sources 3 and 5), so the claim is too general.

Short-term versus long-term: Source 2 shows immediate disruption that mostly recovers, while Source 4 suggests only a small long-term association, so moment-to-moment effects should not be confused with weakened attachment.
Mechanism: Source 4 suggests phone use affects attachment through parental sensitivity, which fits attachment theory and suggests it is unresponsiveness, not the phone itself, that matters.
Measurement: the sources use different measures (behaviour coding, Q-sort, parent-rated closeness, interviews), so they may not be measuring the same thing called 'attachment'.
Causation: only Source 2 is experimental, and it does not measure attachment; the other sources are correlational or qualitative, so cause and effect cannot be established for attachment itself.
Cultural context: Sources 3 and 5 suggest video calls with grandparents and extended family are valued in Gulf families, so the effect of phones may differ across family structures and cultures.
ownKnowledge: Bowlby's attachment theory: the importance of a responsive caregiver and the development of an internal working model.
Ainsworth's Strange Situation and the maternal sensitivity hypothesis, linking sensitive responsiveness to secure attachment.
Tronick's still-face paradigm, which shows infants' distress when a parent becomes unresponsive and their recovery when interaction is repaired.
The concept of 'technoference' (McDaniel and Radesky): everyday interruptions to parent and child interaction caused by technology.
Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's cross-cultural comparison of Strange Situation studies, showing that patterns of attachment vary across cultures.

q1: I explained that Figure 1 gives percentages but no number of children in each group.
I explained why this matters, for example that 33% of a very small group could be only a few children.
I said that the groups are probably unequal in size and that the 'Almost always' bar may be the least reliable.
I focused on interpreting the figure, not on problems with how attachment was measured.
I developed one issue fully instead of listing several.
q2: I compared the phone phase with free play using the means and the t values for all three measures.
I compared t values with the critical value of 2.02 to say which differences were significant.
I commented on the reunion phase and noticed that only bids for attention stayed significantly higher.
I used the SDs, for example the large SD for negative emotion in the phone phase.
I stated a conclusion linked to the claim and noted that the source measures short-term behaviour, not attachment.
I did not claim that the study shows phones cause insecure attachment.
q3: I identified specific sources of bias in Source 3, such as the researcher running a screen-free programme or the leading opening question.
I explained how each bias could be avoided, for example an independent interviewer, a second coder or neutral questions.
I discussed both researcher bias and participant bias (for example social desirability with the other parent present).
I referred to exact details from Source 3, such as recruitment from the workshops and coding by one person.
I wrote in developed paragraphs, not a numbered list.
q4: I used at least three of Sources 2 to 5 and explained what each suggests about the claim.
I evaluated each source, not just described it.
I distinguished between absorbed and shared phone use (Source 5) and between short-term behaviour and attachment (Sources 2 and 4).
I explained what happened in Source 4 when parental sensitivity was controlled.
I used my own knowledge, for example Bowlby, Ainsworth's sensitivity hypothesis or the still-face paradigm.
I reached a reasoned conclusion about the extent to which the claim is supported.

areaOfInquiry: The use of technology to assist with acculturation
title: Social media and settling in
claim: social media helps expatriate families to adapt to life in a new country

sources.title: Newcomer social media groups and feeling settled
text: A relocation services company in Dubai has surveyed samples of about 500 newly arrived expatriate residents. Respondents report whether they belong to an online social media group for newcomers, and whether they felt settled in Dubai after their first 12 months. Figure 1 shows the results of the surveys carried out between 2010 and 2020.

figure.title: Figure 1: Newcomer social media group membership and feeling settled among new expatriate residents in Dubai

series.name: Belong to a newcomer social media group

sources.title: Two kinds of social media use and adaptation
text: Researchers in Abu Dhabi surveyed 212 expatriate parents (124 mothers and 88 fathers, from 31 countries) who had moved to the UAE within the previous three years and had at least one school-age child. Parents reported how many hours per week they spent on two kinds of social media use: host-oriented use (local community, neighbourhood and school parent groups) and home-oriented use (keeping in touch with family, friends and news in their home country).

Parents also completed a sociocultural adaptation scale measuring how easily they manage everyday life in the UAE, such as transport, services and making local contacts (12 to 60; sample mean 41.2, SD 8.3), and a psychological well-being scale (10 to 50; sample mean 36.5, SD 6.1). Higher scores mean better adaptation and well-being. Pearson's correlations were calculated. For this sample, a correlation is significant at p < 0.05 if it is above +0.135 or below -0.135.

table.caption: Table 1: Social media use and its correlation with adaptation and well-being (n = 212)

sources.title: Parents' experiences of a newcomer social media group
text: Researchers held four focus groups in Dubai with 22 expatriate parents (17 mothers and 5 fathers) who had moved to the city within the previous two years. All were members of the same neighbourhood social media group for newcomers and were recruited through a post by the group's administrator. Participants came from India, the United Kingdom, Egypt, the Philippines and South Africa. All had professional jobs, had children at private international schools and spoke English fluently.

The focus groups took place in English at a community centre in 2024. Each lasted about 90 minutes and was led by a researcher who had herself moved to Dubai as an expatriate. Discussions were recorded, transcribed and analysed thematically by two researchers, who compared their codes before agreeing on the final themes.
themes: Theme 1: The group as a first map of the city. Parents used the group for practical advice on schools, doctors, housing and government services.
Theme 2: From online contacts to offline friendships. Posts led to meet-ups, children's playdates and shared school runs.

Theme 3: Living in an expatriate bubble. Contacts made through the group were mainly with other expatriates, often of the same nationality, with little contact with Emirati families or the Arabic language.

quotes.text: Within a week of landing I knew which clinic to take my son to, just from reading the group.
Our children's first playdate came from a post asking if anyone else had just moved to the area.
Everyone in the group is new, like me. It helps, but after a year I realised all my friends are expatriates.
Because I speak Arabic, I used the group less. My neighbours helped me more than the phone did.

sources.title: An online peer group for newly arrived students
text: Researchers in Doha, Qatar, recruited 96 expatriate students aged 13 to 16 who had arrived in Qatar within the previous six months and attended one of three international schools. Students were randomly allocated to two conditions of 48 students each.

In the online peer group condition, each student joined a moderated messaging group of eight to ten students for eight weeks. Each group included two students who had lived in Qatar for more than five years. Moderators posted weekly activities, such as sharing photos of local places and planning a weekend outing. In the control condition, students received the school's usual welcome information.

Loneliness (20 to 80, higher scores mean more lonely) and sociocultural adaptation (12 to 60, higher scores mean better adaptation) were measured before and after the eight weeks. Independent-samples t-tests compared the two conditions after eight weeks (critical value of t(94) at p < 0.05 = 1.99).

table.caption: Table 2: Mean scores before and after eight weeks (SD in brackets)

sources.title: Social media networks and acculturation strategies over 18 months
text: Researchers in Canada followed 418 adults from 14 countries who had recently moved there with their families. Shortly after arrival, participants' social media use was classified into one of three profiles based on who they mainly interacted with online: mostly home-country contacts, a mix of home-country and Canadian contacts, or little social media use.

Eighteen months later, participants completed a questionnaire that classified their acculturation strategy as integration (keeping their own culture while taking part in the new one), assimilation (adopting the new culture and giving up their own), separation (keeping their own culture and avoiding the new one) or marginalisation (taking part in neither).

table.caption: Table 3: Acculturation strategy after 18 months, by social media profile at arrival: number of participants (percentage of profile)
rows: Mix of home-country and Canadian contacts

questions.text: Explain one issue that limits the interpretation of the data in source 1.
Analyse the findings from source 2 and state a conclusion linked to the claim that social media helps expatriate families to adapt to life in a new country.
To what extent are the findings from source 3 transferable to other populations or contexts?
To what extent can we conclude that social media helps expatriate families to adapt to life in a new country? In your answer, use your own knowledge and at least three of sources 2 to 5.

issues: The survey years are plotted as evenly spaced points although the real gaps are 5, 3, 1 and 1 years, so the slopes are misleading: the rise from 2010 to 2015 (23 points over five years, about 4.6 points a year) is drawn as the steepest part of the line, while the rise from 2019 to 2020 (8 points in a single year) looks gentler even though it was faster per year.
Because of the unequal intervals, a reader may think group membership and feeling settled grew at a steady rate, when the yearly rate of change was actually much faster in the later years.
The lines join points across missing years (2011 to 2014 and 2016 to 2017), suggesting smooth change where there are no data, so any rises or falls in those years are hidden.

Both trends are shown on the same graph, which invites the reader to link them, but these are yearly percentages for different respondents, so the figure cannot show whether the people in groups were the ones who felt settled.
'Felt settled' is not defined in the figure, so it is unclear what the second line is measuring.
The figure does not show how many people answered each year, so small differences between adjacent years (for example 66% and 68%) may not be meaningful.

analysis: Host-oriented use had a moderate positive correlation with sociocultural adaptation (r = +0.41, p < 0.001), the strongest relationship in the table; this is well above the critical value of 0.135.
Host-oriented use also had a weak positive correlation with psychological well-being (r = +0.22, p = 0.001).
Home-oriented use was not significantly related to sociocultural adaptation: r = -0.12 lies between -0.135 and +0.135 (p = 0.08), although the direction is negative.

Home-oriented use did have a weak positive, significant correlation with psychological well-being (r = +0.19, p = 0.006), so keeping in touch with home was linked to feeling better but not to managing everyday life in the UAE.

Parents spent more than twice as long on home-oriented use (7.9 hours) as on host-oriented use (3.6 hours); the SD of 2.9 for host use relative to its mean suggests the data are positively skewed, with many low users.
Even the strongest correlation (+0.41) shares only about 17% of variance, and correlations cannot show that social media use causes better adaptation.
conclusion: The findings partly support the claim: host-oriented social media use was linked to better sociocultural adaptation and well-being among expatriate parents in Abu Dhabi.
The support depends on the kind of social media use: home-oriented use was linked to well-being but not to adaptation, so social media in general does not appear to help adaptation equally.
Because the data are correlational, it is equally possible that parents who adapt well join more local groups, so the conclusion should be stated as an association, not a cause.

points: Population: all 22 participants were professional, English-speaking parents with children at private international schools, so the findings may not transfer to lower-income expatriates, workers without families in the country, or people who do not speak English.

Self-selection: participants were members of one newcomer group recruited by its administrator, so they are likely to be active, positive users; the findings may not transfer to expatriates who do not use such groups or who left them.

Context: Dubai has a very large expatriate population and well-established online newcomer networks, so findings may not transfer to countries where migrants are a small minority or where such groups do not exist.

Language and cultural distance: Participant 20 (Arabic-speaking, from Egypt) relied on the group less than others, suggesting the role of social media depends on how familiar the host culture is, which limits transfer between groups of migrants.
Gender and family role: 17 of 22 participants were mothers and no children were included, so the findings may not transfer to fathers or to the adolescents of expatriate families.
Time: the focus groups took place in 2024 with one platform's group, so the findings may not transfer to earlier periods or to different platforms.

In favour of transferability: the detailed description of participants and setting allows readers to judge similarity to other contexts, and the 'expatriate bubble' theme fits Berry's separation strategy, a pattern found in many cultures, which supports theoretical transfer of the themes.

sources: Source 2 partly supports the claim: host-oriented use was moderately linked to sociocultural adaptation, but home-oriented use was not. Limitation: correlational self-report survey, so direction of cause is unclear.

Source 3 supports the claim in the early months (practical help, offline friendships) but also shows a possible 'expatriate bubble' with little contact with the host culture. Limitation: a small, self-selected, English-speaking professional sample from one group.

Source 4 supports the claim: a moderated online peer group that included longer-term residents reduced loneliness in newly arrived adolescents, though the effect on adaptation was not significant. Limitation: eight weeks only, adolescents rather than whole families, and a structured, moderated group unlike everyday social media.

Source 5 challenges a general version of the claim: newcomers who mainly used social media with home-country contacts were more likely to adopt separation, while those with mixed contacts were more likely to integrate. Limitation: social media profile and strategy were not manipulated, and the setting is Canada.
discussion: Who people connect with online matters more than social media itself: host-oriented or mixed networks are linked to adaptation and integration (Sources 2, 4 and 5), while home-oriented networks may support well-being but encourage separation (Sources 2 and 5).

Psychological and sociocultural adaptation can differ: home-oriented use was linked to well-being but not to everyday adaptation (Source 2), and the online group reduced loneliness more than it improved adaptation (Source 4).

Social media may help with practical adjustment early on but create an expatriate bubble that limits contact with the host culture (Source 3), so the claim may depend on how long families have been in the country.
Only Source 4 is experimental, and it tests a structured, moderated group, which is not the same as ordinary social media use; Sources 2 and 5 are correlational.

Context matters: Dubai and Doha have large expatriate populations, which may make expatriate-to-expatriate networks a normal route to settling in, unlike countries such as Canada where integration with the majority culture may be expected.
The meaning of 'adapt' is debatable: some families may prefer separation or a temporary stay, so whether reduced contact with the host culture is a problem depends on their goals.
ownKnowledge: Berry's acculturation model (integration, assimilation, separation, marginalisation) and the concept of acculturative stress.
Ward and colleagues' distinction between psychological adaptation and sociocultural adaptation.
Bonding and bridging social capital (Putnam), and Ellison, Steinfield and Lampe's (2007) finding that Facebook use was associated with bridging social capital among university students.
Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner): online groups of the same nationality may strengthen in-group identity.
Allport's contact hypothesis: contact with members of the host community under supportive conditions can improve intergroup relations.

areaOfInquiry: The effect of technology on cognition
title: AI tools and critical thinking
claim: using AI tools reduces students' critical thinking

sources.title: AI chatbot use for homework and a critical thinking task
text: Researchers surveyed 438 secondary school students aged 15 to 17 in Ras Al Khaimah about how often they used AI chatbots to help with their homework. During a normal lesson, the students then completed a critical thinking task set by the researchers. Figure 1 shows the mean result for each group of students.

figure.title: Figure 1: Critical thinking task results by frequency of AI chatbot use for homework
figure.xLabel: Frequency of AI chatbot use for homework

sources.title: Writing with and without an AI chatbot
text: Researchers in Sharjah carried out a four-week experiment with 64 Grade 11 students (34 girls and 30 boys, aged 16 to 17) from two schools. Students were randomly allocated to two conditions of 32 students. Each week, all students wrote an argumentative essay on a social issue in a 50-minute lesson. In the AI condition, students could use an AI chatbot in any way they wished while writing. In the no-AI condition, students could use only printed source material. Two teachers who did not know which condition each student was in marked the essays out of 20. After each essay, students rated their mental effort from 1 (very little) to 9 (very high).

In week five, all students completed an argument evaluation test without any AI support. In this test, students judged the strength of arguments and identified flaws in reasoning (scored 0 to 30, higher scores indicate better critical thinking). Independent-samples t-tests compared the conditions (critical value of t(62) at p < 0.05 = 2.00).

sources.title: Conversations about AI use and thinking
text: A study of participants in the United Kingdom investigated whether the amount of AI tool use was related to cognitive offloading (using external tools to handle mental tasks that people could otherwise complete themselves) and to critical thinking. A total of 666 participants were recruited online through various social media platforms. They ranged from high school graduates to people with doctoral degrees and came from a variety of professional fields. When signing up, participants were told that their names and identities would be kept secure and would not be published.

All participants completed a questionnaire of 23 prompts on a 6-point Likert scale, measuring how often they used AI tools, how heavily they relied on digital devices for memory and problem-solving, and how they used critical thinking skills in everyday situations. The researchers then selected a smaller subset of 50 participants for more detailed one-on-one conversations, in which participants described their daily routines and explained how AI influenced their problem-solving and decision-making. The conversations were transcribed word for word and systematically coded to find overarching patterns and themes about cognitive dependence. For analysis, participants were grouped by age: younger (17 to 25 years), middle-aged (26 to 45 years) and older (46 years and older).
themes: Theme 1: Dependence on AI among younger participants. Younger participants described a high dependence on AI for both routine and complex tasks and openly admitted that they felt they were losing their ability to think deeply.
Theme 2: Independent problem-solving among older participants. Older participants preferred traditional, independent problem-solving to keep their cognitive skills sharp.

Theme 3: Shared concern about critical thinking. Participants across all age groups were concerned that relying on AI was reducing their ability to think critically and solve problems independently; younger participants were particularly concerned that easy access to AI reduced their inclination to engage in deep thinking.
sources.citation: Gerlich, M. (2025). AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking. Societies, 15(1), 6. https://doi.org/10.3390/soc15010006

sources.title: How students use AI and critical thinking test scores
text: Researchers surveyed 540 first-year university students aged 18 to 21 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Doha, Qatar. Students reported how many hours per week they used AI tools for their coursework, and how much of this time was answer-seeking (asking the AI to produce answers, summaries or essays) or feedback-seeking (asking the AI to question, check or criticise their own work). They then completed a timed critical thinking test that involved evaluating evidence and arguments (scored 0 to 40, higher scores indicate better critical thinking). Their final school grades were also collected.

For this sample, a correlation is significant at p < 0.05 if it is above +0.085 or below -0.085. Students' final school grades were positively correlated with feedback-seeking use (r = +0.27, p < 0.001).

table.caption: Table 2: AI use for coursework and correlation with critical thinking test scores (n = 540)

sources.title: A questioning AI tutor in science lessons
text: Researchers in Singapore randomly allocated 150 students aged 14 to 15 to three conditions for six weekly science reasoning lessons. In the questioning AI condition, students worked with an AI tutor set up never to give answers, but instead to ask questions, request evidence and point out gaps in the student's reasoning. In the standard AI condition, students used an AI chatbot with no restrictions. In the no-AI condition, students worked from textbooks.

All students completed a critical thinking test (scored 0 to 50, higher scores indicate better critical thinking) before the first lesson and after the last one. A one-way ANOVA on the gains found a significant difference between conditions: F(2, 147) = 9.84, p < 0.001 (critical value of F = 3.06). Follow-up comparisons showed that the questioning AI group gained significantly more than both other groups (p < 0.01), while the standard AI and no-AI groups did not differ significantly (p = 0.19).

questions.text: Explain one issue that limits the interpretation of the data in source 1.
Analyse the findings from source 2 and state a conclusion linked to the claim that using AI tools reduces students' critical thinking.
Discuss how the researcher could avoid bias in source 3.
To what extent can we conclude that using AI tools reduces students' critical thinking? In your answer, use your own knowledge and at least three of sources 2 to 5.

issues: The y-axis is labelled only 'Score', with no explanation of what the score measures, its maximum or its units, so the reader cannot tell whether the fall from 6.8 to 5.1 is a large or small difference.

Because the direction of the scale is not stated, the reader cannot be sure whether a higher score means better critical thinking or, for example, more errors, so even the direction of the relationship is uncertain.
The axis runs to 10, but nothing says the task was scored out of 10; if the maximum were much higher (for example 50 or 100), all four groups would be very close together.
The text gives no information about the critical thinking task, so the reader cannot tell which aspect of critical thinking the score represents.
No error bars, standard deviations or group sizes are shown, so the reader cannot judge whether the differences between groups are meaningful.
The frequency categories are vague (for example 'Weekly' could mean once or several times a week), which makes it hard to interpret the trend across the bars.

analysis: Students in the AI condition produced better essays (mean 15.2 vs 12.4 out of 20), a significant difference (t = 4.74, greater than 2.00), so AI improved the product while it was available.
Students in the AI condition reported much less mental effort (3.9 vs 6.2 on a 9-point scale, t = 6.12), suggesting they offloaded some of the thinking to the chatbot.

On the argument evaluation test without AI, the AI condition scored 2.9 points lower (16.4 vs 19.3 out of 30); t = 2.58 is greater than the critical value of 2.00 (p = 0.012), so the difference is significant.

The SDs on the test (4.6 and 4.4) are larger than the difference between the means, and the ranges overlap heavily (7 to 26 and 10 to 28), so many students in the AI condition scored higher than many in the no-AI condition.
The AI condition had a lower minimum (7) and a slightly wider spread, suggesting the effect may not have been the same for all students.

The pattern across the three measures (better essays, less effort, weaker independent test performance) is consistent with cognitive offloading, but the study did not measure how each student used the chatbot.
conclusion: The findings support the claim: students who used an AI chatbot freely for four weeks then performed significantly worse on an independent critical thinking test than students who did not.

A more cautious conclusion is that unrestricted AI use during writing improved essays but was associated with lower effort and lower independent argument evaluation, so it may reduce the practice of critical thinking rather than the ability itself.
Because the effect was moderate, the scores overlapped and the study lasted only four weeks, it supports the claim for short-term, unrestricted use rather than for AI use in general.

points: Researcher bias in coding: the study was designed around concerns about cognitive offloading, so the researchers may have looked for evidence of dependence; using several independent coders, checking agreement between them and keeping a record of coding decisions would reduce this.

Selection of interviewees: the source does not say how the 50 participants were chosen from the 666; choosing them randomly, or purposively across age groups and levels of AI use and reporting the method, would avoid selecting people who fit the researchers' expectations.

Leading topics and demand characteristics: conversations focused on how AI influenced problem-solving may signal that the researchers expected a negative effect; neutral, open questions that also ask about benefits of AI would reduce participant bias.

Coding by age group: because participants were grouped by age, coders' expectations about younger and older people could influence interpretation; coding transcripts without knowing the participant's age group would reduce this.
Sampling bias: recruiting online through social media platforms may attract heavy technology users or people with strong views about AI; using a wider range of recruitment methods would reduce this.
Credit the existing step against participant bias: keeping identities secure reduces social desirability, and this could be strengthened by an interviewer not linked to the study's hypothesis.
Reflexivity: the researchers could report their own views on AI and how these might have shaped the conversations and themes.

sources: Source 2 supports the claim: after four weeks of unrestricted chatbot use, students scored significantly lower on an independent argument evaluation test and reported less mental effort. Limitation: short study with two schools in Sharjah, and the AI could be used in any way, so the type of use was not controlled.

Source 3 supports the claim from users' own perspectives: participants, especially younger ones, felt AI was reducing their ability and inclination to think deeply. Limitation: self-reports of perceived decline, not measured ability, with possible researcher bias and a UK sample aged 17 and over recruited online.

Source 4 complicates the claim: answer-seeking use was negatively correlated with critical thinking, but feedback-seeking use was positively correlated. Limitation: correlational, and students with higher school grades used AI more for feedback, which could explain the positive link.

Source 5 challenges the claim: a questioning AI tutor produced the largest gains in critical thinking, and the standard AI group did not differ significantly from the no-AI group. Limitation: one subject, six lessons and a carefully designed tutor that is unlike most AI tools students use.
discussion: How AI is used matters: using AI to obtain answers is linked to lower critical thinking (Sources 2 and 4), while using AI to question and give feedback is linked to better critical thinking (Sources 4 and 5).
Cognitive offloading explains several findings: lower effort and weaker independent performance (Source 2) and participants' concerns about losing deep thinking (Source 3).

Performance with AI and learning from AI are different: AI improved essay marks (Source 2) while reducing later independent performance, so judging AI by the quality of work produced may be misleading.
The strength of the evidence varies: experiments (Sources 2 and 5) allow causal conclusions but are short-term; Sources 3 and 4 show associations and perceptions from different populations.

Population and context: sources include Gulf secondary and university students, UK adults and Singaporean students, so findings about age (younger participants in Source 3) and education level may not generalise.
Whether the reduction is lasting is unclear: none of the sources measure critical thinking over months or years.
ownKnowledge: Cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert, 2016): using external tools to reduce cognitive demand, which can free resources but may reduce practice of the skill.
The 'Google effect' (Sparrow, Liu and Wegner, 2011): people remember less information when they expect to be able to look it up later.
Levels of processing (Craik and Lockhart, 1972) and 'desirable difficulties' (Bjork): effortful processing produces stronger learning.
Dual-process theory (Kahneman's System 1 and System 2): critical thinking relies on effortful System 2 processing, which AI answers may allow students to skip.
Cognitive load theory (Sweller): well-designed support can reduce unnecessary load and help learning, which fits the questioning tutor in Source 5.
